fetched_contents.text: CKD staging * 4 variable Kidney Failure Risk Equation * CKD Stages G1 or G2 * CKD Stage G3 * CKD Stages G4 and G5 CKD Classification A patient is said to have chronic kidney disease (CKD) if they have abnormalities of kidney function or structure present for more than 3 months. The definition of CKD includes all individuals with markers of kidney damage (see below*) or those with an eGFR of less than 60 ml/min/1.73m² on at least 2 occasions 90 days apart (with or without markers of kidney damage). * *Markers of kidney disease may include: albuminuria (ACR > 3 mg/mmol), haematuria (of presumed or confirmed renal origin), electrolyte abnormalities due to tubular disorders, renal histological abnormalities, structural abnormalities detected by imaging (e.g. polycystic kidneys, reflux nephropathy) or a history of kidney transplantation. CKD Classification CKD is classified based on the eGFR and the level of proteinuria and helps to risk stratify patients. Patients are classified as G1-G5, based on the eGFR, and A1-A3 based on the ACR (albumin:creatinine ratio) as detailed below: For Example * A person with an eGFR of 25 ml/min/1.73m² and an ACR of 15 mg/mmol has CKD G4A2. * A person with an eGFR of 50 ml/min/1.73m² and an ACR of 35 mg/mmol has CKD G3aA3. It is important to note that patients with an eGFR of >60 ml/min/1.73m² should not be classified as having CKD unless they have other markers of kidney disease (see above*). Patient information Patients with CKD can be classified depending on their level of kidney function, or eGFR, and the amount of protein present in the urine. This information forms the basis of CKD staging which is useful for planning follow up and management. The higher the stage (G1->G5) and the greater the amount of protein present in the urine (A1->A3) the more "severe" the CKD and the higher the risk that a patient may develop renal failure requiring dialysis in the future. Kidney Failure Risk Equation (KFRE) What is the Kidney Failure Risk Equation? The Kidney Failure Risk Equation (KFRE) is a well-validated risk prediction tool for a kidney replacement therapy (KRT) in the next two or five years in individuals with chronic kidney disease (CKD) stages 3a-5. To estimate the risk of KRT, the four-variable KFRE uses: * Age * Sex * Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) * Urine albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR) The KFRE has been re-calibrated specifically for the UK population and is available via this website. Please note that this may be different from some other publicly available calculators. When should the Kidney Failure Risk Equation be calculated? The KFRE should be calculated when an individual with CKD Stage 3a-5 has an eGFR and ACR measured. This should be at least on an annual basis, but more frequently with more advanced disease (see the frequency of monitoring section of management of patients with CKD). We would recommend that both eGFR and ACR should be within six months of each other, and ideally within a month. How will the Kidney Failure Risk Equation improve care for my patients? * The UK re-calibrated KFRE has recently been recommended by NICE to guide personalised care for people with CKD stages 3a-5 including referral to secondary care. If the risk of KRT is >5% in the next 5 years, referral should be considered factoring in the patient's 'wishes and comorbidities'. This threshold has replaced the previous recommendation for considering referral if eGFR is less than 30 ml/min/1.73m². This is because it is likely to be more sensitive and specific for KRT and may reduce the number of people referred unnecessarily. * Two-year predictions may be more applicable to secondary care when discussing the risk of requiring KRT over a shorter timeframe and planning for procedures such as fistula formation or transplant listing. How do I communicate Kidney Failure Risk Equation scores with patients? Discussing KRT risk with should follow NICE's guidelines for 'shared decision making' and should include: * Discussing KRT risk in the context of a patient's life, such as comorbidities and what matters most to the patient * Describing KRT risk over the appropriate timeframe using 'natural frequencies' such as '10 in 100', instead of percentages such as '10%' * Use a mixture of numbers and pictures What are some limitations of the Kidney Failure Risk Equation? * As KFRE uses eGFR and urine ACR to make a prediction, the same limitations for eGFR and urine ACR are also applicable to KFRE. Examples include assessment of patients at extremes of weight or muscle mass, or where a patient is being assessed in the context of acute kidney injury, or for ACR where a patient has a urinary tract infection. Please see the measurement of kidney function sections on eGFR and albuminuria for further explanation. * KFRE should always be viewed in the context of the individual, their comorbidities, and their risk of dying from other causes over a period of the next two/five years. * There has been limited specific validation of the KFRE in primary renal pathologies such as glomerulonephritis, cystic kidney disease and vasculitis. Therefore, in these groups caution should be used when making predictions based on KFRE. More detailed information on KFRE including its development is available here. fetched_contents.text: Stage 3a CKD: Mild to Moderate Kidney Function Loss Explained Stage 3a CKD: Learn about mild to moderate kidney function loss, symptoms, lifestyle changes, diet, medications, and steps to manage and lower your health risks. About Stage 3a CKD Stage 3a CKD means you have mild to moderate loss of kidney function. People with stage 3a CKD have an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) between 45 and 59 for 3 months or more (confirmed with repeat testing to make sure you don't have acute kidney injury). Another way to think about these numbers is your kidneys are working at 45-59% of what the average two healthy kidneys in a young person can do. This is the first stage of CKD where blood test results alone can confirm a diagnosis of CKD. Although urine albumin-creatinine ratio (uACR) results are not needed to confirm CKD at this stage, getting your uACR checked is still very important to gain a full picture of your kidney health, as shown in the graphic below. Although this is the third stage of CKD, stages 3a and 3b are when most people with CKD are first diagnosed. Health risks with stage 3a CKD In stage 3a CKD, you are at increased risk for your CKD getting worse and you are at risk for heart disease (even if your uACR is lower than 30). As your uACR number goes up, your risks of developing heart disease and CKD progression (worsening) both go up dramatically (as seen in the figure below). CKD complications Stage 3a CKD is also when complications from chronic kidney disease can start to appear, although the risk at this stage is very low. These complications include: * Anemia (low levels of red blood cells) * Mineral and bone disorder (when blood levels of calcium and phosphorus are out of balance leading to bone and/or heart disease) * Metabolic acidosis (buildup of acid in the blood) Although the risk of having these complications is very low when you are in stage 3a CKD, guidelines recommend getting screened now to make sure everything is okay (if you haven't been screened yet). Screening for each of these complications can be done with simple blood tests ordered by your healthcare professional. People with stage 3a CKD are also at increased risk of developing high blood pressure. So, it is important to have your blood pressure checked regularly. Signs and symptoms Stage 3a CKD is when symptoms may start to appear, but typically no symptoms are present. Some of these symptoms may include: * Urinating (peeing) more often or less often than usual * Itchy and/or dry skin * Feeling tired * Nausea * Loss of appetite * Weight loss without trying to lose weight Lifestyle recommendations Now is a great time to make healthier lifestyle choices: * If you smoke and/or use tobacco products, stop. Smoking can speed up the kidney disease process and increase your risk of getting kidney failure. It also increases your risk for other serious health problems, including high blood pressure, heart disease, cancers, and stroke. * Exercise regularly. Remember, it’s okay to start slowly – taking short walks is a great way to begin. * Sleeping well is important, too. Try to get enough sleep so you are well-rested. * If you are overweight, losing weight through a balanced diet and physical activity can help improve your health in many ways. * Find ways to reduce and manage stress in your life. Nutrition With stage 3a CKD, you may need to start changing the kinds of foods you eat. If you have high blood pressure, it is important to limit your sodium (salt) intake to less than 2300 mg per day (about 1 teaspoon of salt from all the food and drinks you consume each day). Your healthcare provider may advise an even lower target depending on your other health conditions. This means a lot more than not using a saltshaker, but also limiting foods with high levels of sodium listed on their nutrition facts label. Some foods that don’t taste salty can have a surprising amount of sodium when you check their nutrition facts label. Based on the results of your blood tests, your healthcare professional or kidney dietitian may also advise you to change how much potassium, phosphorus, and/or calcium you might be getting through your diet. Recommendations are highly customized to your body’s specific needs and dietary preferences. Ask your healthcare professional or kidney dietitian about potential dietary recommendations tailored to you. Meeting with a dietitian can be especially helpful if you also have other health conditions like high blood pressure, diabetes, or heart failure where it is even more important to integrate a healthy diet into your lifestyle to help prevent complications. It can feel overwhelming to keep track of so many changes, and a dietitian can help you identify what works best for you. Additional information about eating healthy with kidney disease can be found on the Nutrition and Early Kidney Disease page. Medications In stage 3a CKD, some of your medications may start to build up in your body. This is because about half of all FDA-approved medications are removed from the blood by your kidneys. Ask your healthcare professional or pharmacist if any of your medication doses need to be lowered because of your stage 3a CKD. Some medications may be best avoided or limited in use as well. Your healthcare professional may prescribe one or more medicines to help slow down or stop your CKD from getting worse. These medicines include an ACE inhibitor/ARB, an SGLT2 inhibitor and/or an nsMRA. Your healthcare professional may also prescribe a statin (cholesterol medicine). Guidelines recommend a statin for people with stage 3a CKD who also have diabetes, a history of heart disease, or are age 50 or older. Even if you do not have high cholesterol, a statin can help lower your risk of having a heart attack or stroke. Stage 3 kidney disease means your kidneys are moderately damaged and not working as well as they should, but it does not yet mean dialysis or kidney transplant is needed [N1-R2]. The key functional classification is based on estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). Stage 3 is divided into two subgroups: stage 3A is eGFR 45–59 mL/min/1.73 m², and stage 3B is eGFR 30–44 mL/min/1.73 m² [N1-R3][N1-R5]. In other words, stage 3A means mild to moderate loss of kidney function, while stage 3B means more severe loss of function than stage 3A but still less severe than stage 4 or 5 [N1-F1].

The main difference between stage 3A and 3B is the degree of kidney function loss. Stage 3A is the lower end of moderate kidney damage, while stage 3B is the upper end of moderate damage and is closer to the next stages of decline [N1-R3][N1-R5]. The UK Kidney Association explicitly states that stage G3 patients have impaired kidney function and that eGFR is the central measure used to classify CKD [N1-F1]. The staging system also uses urine albuminuria and other markers to refine risk and guide care, but eGFR remains the core criterion [N1-R4].

A stage 3 diagnosis matters because it signals that kidney damage is already present and that the disease is progressing, even if the damage is not yet advanced. The evidence emphasizes that stage 3 is when complications from chronic kidney disease can start to appear, though the risk at this stage is generally low [N1-F1]. The Kidney Failure Risk Equation (KFRE) is specifically designed for CKD stages 3a–5 and is used to estimate the risk of needing kidney replacement therapy, which helps explain why stage 3 is not merely a benign early stage but a clinically meaningful point where future risk and management planning become important [N1-F1]. In short, stage 3 means your kidneys are damaged enough to need attention, but dialysis is not yet required [N1-R2][N1-F1].

For stage 3 kidney disease, referral to a nephrologist is not automatic but is guided by risk and the need for specialized management. The evidence shows that referral criteria often include signs of rapid progression, hereditary kidney disease, hematuria, nephrotic syndrome, or high risk of progression to end-stage renal disease (ESRD), not only eGFR thresholds [N2-R4]. Some guidelines suggest referral when eGFR is consistently <30 mL/min/1.73 m² or when the likelihood of kidney replacement therapy is high, but the evidence here also notes that modern guidance may be more nuanced than a single GFR cutoff [N2-R1]. The UK Kidney Association’s material also says that referrals should be considered if the Kidney Failure Risk Equation (KFRE) suggests a >5% risk of KRT in the next 5 years, which is now the recommended approach rather than waiting for eGFR <30 [N1-F1].

Dialysis planning or specialized care becomes relevant when the disease is no longer just stage 3 and the risk of needing dialysis rises. The evidence explicitly says that dialysis is generally considered for patients with stage 5 CKD, not stage 3 [N4-R1][N4-R3]. However, the KFRE is used for stages 3a–5 to estimate when kidney replacement therapy may be needed, so stage 3 patients can still be referred early if their risk profile indicates that dialysis planning should begin [N1-F1]. In other words, stage 3 itself does not mean dialysis is imminent, but it can be a signal to start specialist care and plan for future needs if risk is high [N1-F1][N4-R3].

At a specialist visit, the patient can expect a comprehensive assessment of kidney function, urine protein, and other markers of kidney damage, plus a discussion of heart disease risk, complications, lifestyle changes, diet, and medications [N2-F2]. The evidence also says that patients with stage 3a CKD may need changes in medications, sodium intake, potassium/phosphorus/calcium balance, and regular monitoring of anemia, mineral and bone disorder, metabolic acidosis, and high blood pressure [N2-F2]. Specialist care is therefore not just about labeling stage 3; it is about slowing progression, preventing complications, and preparing for longer-term kidney health decisions [N2-R4][N2-F2].

The patient should ask their doctor several specific next steps to reduce uncertainty. The evidence supports asking what stage the eGFR places them in, what caused their kidney disease, and whether further kidney damage can be prevented [N5-R3][N5-R5]. It also suggests asking what lab test results are, including GFR, and whether changes in kidney function have occurred since last testing [N5-R4]. A helpful question is also whether there are lifestyle or dietary changes needed, and whether any medications need adjustment because of kidney function [N5-R3][N5-R4].

To track kidney function over time, the patient should focus on regular eGFR measurements and urine albuminuria tests, because the evidence says that eGFR and ACR are used together to stage CKD and that repeat testing confirms the diagnosis [N1-R4][N1-F1]. The evidence also emphasizes that ACR is important even if not needed to confirm stage 3a CKD, because it gives a fuller picture of kidney health [N2-F2]. The patient should therefore ask how often follow-up tests are needed and whether blood pressure, anemia, mineral and bone disorder, metabolic acidosis, and other complications will be monitored [N1-F1][N2-F2].

To prepare for a specialist visit, the patient should bring an updated list of medications, vitamins, supplements, and herbal medicines, and be ready to discuss lifestyle, diet, and any symptoms [N5-R3][N5-R5]. They should also ask what they can expect from the visit, what tests will be done, and what the specialist will recommend [N5-R1][N5-R4]. The evidence also supports asking how to slow disease progression and what steps can be taken to protect kidney health [N5-R3]. Overall, the next steps are to seek clarity on the diagnosis, get a plan for monitoring and lifestyle changes, and prepare for a specialist visit with detailed questions about testing, risk, and management [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R4].

In Lagos, there are both local clinics and specialized nephrology/dialysis centers available, but the evidence suggests a clear distinction between them. The local clinic-like options are more general, while the specialized centers are dedicated to kidney disease, dialysis, and related services. Lagos-specific sources show that hospitals and centers such as Lagos State University Teaching Hospital (LASUTH) Special Services Centre, St. Raphael Divine Mercy Specialist Hospital, CardioCare Hospital, and other institutions offer nephrology consultations, dialysis services, and related treatments [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5][N6-R3][N6-R5]. These specialized centers are designed for people with kidney disease, including acute or chronic kidney disease, dialysis access, kidney biopsies, and other advanced services [N3-R3][N6-R1].

The evidence indicates that local clinics can manage basic care and follow-up, but they may not have the full range of nephrology services needed for stage 3 disease. The UK Kidney Association material says that CKD staging and management require follow-up planning and that referral to secondary care may be appropriate when risk is high [N1-F1]. In Lagos, that means local clinics may be able to monitor routine kidney function, check urine albuminuria, and manage basic symptoms, but they may not be the best place for specialist assessment of stage 3 disease [N1-R4][N1-F1]. Specialized centers, by contrast, can provide nephrology consultations, dialysis planning, kidney biopsies, and other advanced diagnostic and treatment services [N3-R2][N3-R3][N6-R1].

What local care can and cannot do for stage 3 depends on the clinic’s resources. The evidence suggests that local care can confirm a stage 3 diagnosis and begin monitoring, but stage 3 is a point where specialist referral is often needed because of the risk of progression and complications [N2-R4][N1-F1]. Local clinics may not have the expertise or equipment to manage complications like anemia, mineral and bone disorder, metabolic acidosis, or high blood pressure as comprehensively as a specialized nephrology center [N2-F2]. Therefore, for early stage 3, local clinics can serve as the starting point, but specialist care is more appropriate when the diagnosis is established and the patient needs a personalized plan for slowing disease and managing future risks [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## Short answer to your question

No, stage 3 kidney disease does **not** mean you automatically go straight to a specialized dialysis center. Based on the evidence, **local clinics can manage early stage 3 kidney disease as part of care**, but they may not be the best place for the full specialist workup you need when the diagnosis is established. You may still be referred to a nephrologist or specialized center, especially if the doctor believes your risk of progression or complications is higher [N2-R4][N1-F1].

## What stage 3 kidney disease really means

Stage 3 means your kidneys are moderately damaged and not working as well as they should, but dialysis or transplant is not yet needed [N1-R2]. The key numbers are estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR):  
- **Stage 3A**: eGFR 45–59 mL/min/1.73 m²  
- **Stage 3B**: eGFR 30–44 mL/min/1.73 m²  

So stage 3A is mild to moderate loss of kidney function, while stage 3B is more severe loss within the same overall stage group [N1-R3][N1-R5]. The staging system also uses urine albuminuria and other markers to guide care, but eGFR remains the central classification measure [N1-R4].  

What matters most is that stage 3 is not harmless. The evidence says stage 3 is when complications from chronic kidney disease can start to appear, though the risk is generally low at this stage [N1-F1]. That is why your doctor likely wants to monitor you closely and decide whether specialist care is needed.

## When you should be referred to a specialist

Referral to a nephrologist is not automatic. It is usually guided by risk, progression, or specific findings such as hematuria, hereditary kidney disease, high risk of progressing to end-stage renal disease (ESRD), nephrotic syndrome, or rapidly worsening disease [N2-R4]. Some guidelines also use the Kidney Failure Risk Equation (KFRE) to help decide when referral is appropriate, especially if the risk of needing kidney replacement therapy is >5% in the next 5 years [N1-F1].

Dialysis planning or specialized care becomes relevant when the disease moves closer to advanced stages or when the risk of needing dialysis rises. The evidence says dialysis is generally considered for stage 5 CKD, not stage 3 [N4-R1][N4-R3]. So, for stage 3, a specialist visit is more about slowing progression, managing complications, and planning for the future, not about starting dialysis [N2-F2][N1-F1].

At a specialist visit, you can expect a full review of your kidney function, urine protein, heart disease risk, and other complications. You may also get recommendations for lifestyle changes, diet, medications, and monitoring for anemia, mineral and bone disorder, metabolic acidosis, and high blood pressure [N2-F2]. In other words, the specialist helps you move from diagnosis to a personalized plan for slowing the disease.

## What local clinics and Lagos clinics can do

In Lagos, there are both general local clinics and specialized nephrology/dialysis centers available [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5][N6-R3][N6-R5]. The evidence shows that hospitals and centers such as Lagos State University Teaching Hospital (LASUTH), St. Raphael Divine Mercy Specialist Hospital, CardioCare Hospital, and other facilities offer nephrology consultations, dialysis services, and related treatments [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5][N6-R1]. These specialized centers can handle kidney biopsies, dialysis access, and other advanced services [N6-R1].

So, local clinics can help monitor routine kidney function and provide basic follow-up, but they may not be the best place to start specialist care for stage 3 disease. The evidence suggests that local clinics may not manage complications such as anemia, mineral and bone disorder, metabolic acidosis, or high blood pressure as comprehensively as a specialized nephrology center [N2-F2][N1-F1]. That means local clinics can be a good starting point, but specialist care is more appropriate when the diagnosis is confirmed and you need a full plan [N1-F1][N2-R4].

## What you can do now: next steps and questions

If you want to reduce uncertainty, ask your doctor these kinds of questions:  
- What stage does my eGFR put me in?  
- What caused my kidney disease?  
- Can I prevent further kidney damage?  
- What changes should I make to my lifestyle, diet, or medications?  
- What lab test results do I have, and have they changed since last time?  
- What will happen next, and how often should I be checked?  
- Should I see a nephrologist, and why? [N5-R3][N5-R5][N5-R4]

To track kidney function over time, focus on regular eGFR and urine albuminuria testing, because those are the main markers used to stage CKD and monitor progression [N1-R4][N1-F1]. The evidence also says that urine albuminuria is important even if not needed to confirm stage 3a CKD [N2-F2].

To prepare for a specialist visit, bring an updated list of medications, vitamins, supplements, and herbal medicines, and be ready to discuss lifestyle, diet, and any symptoms you are having [N5-R3][N5-R4]. Ask what tests the specialist will do and what they expect to find [N5-R1]. That way, you can go in with questions and a clearer picture of what comes next.

## Bottom line

Stage 3 kidney disease means your kidneys are moderately damaged, but dialysis is not yet needed [N1-R2]. Local clinics can manage early stage 3 as part of care, but specialist nephrology care is often needed when the diagnosis is established and risk is higher [N1-F1][N2-R4]. In Lagos, there are specialized nephrology and dialysis centers available, so your doctor can choose the best setting for your case [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5][N6-R1]. If you are unsure, the best next step is to ask your doctor what testing, monitoring, and specialist care are needed, and then prepare for a visit with specific questions [N5-R3][N5-R4].

## What stage 3 kidney disease really means

Stage 3 means your kidneys are moderately damaged and not working as well as they should, but dialysis or transplant is not yet needed [N1-R2]. The key numbers are estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR):  
- **Stage 3A**: eGFR 45–59 mL/min/1.73 m²  
- **Stage 3B**: eGFR 30–44 mL/min/1.73 m²

The evidence says stage 3 is when complications from chronic kidney disease can start to appear, though the risk is generally low at this stage [N1-F1]. That is why your doctor likely wants to monitor you closely and decide whether specialist care is needed.

Referral to a nephrologist is not automatic. It is usually guided by risk, progression, or specific findings such as hematuria, hereditary kidney disease, high risk of progressing to end-stage renal disease (ESRD), nephrotic syndrome, or rapidly worsening disease [N2-R4]. - What caused my kidney disease?

The evidence says stage 3 is when complications from chronic kidney disease can start to appear, though the risk is generally low at this stage [N1-F1]. That is why your doctor likely wants to monitor you closely and decide whether specialist care is needed.

## When you should be referred to a specialist

Referral to a nephrologist is not automatic. It is usually guided by risk, progression, or specific findings such as hematuria, hereditary kidney disease, high risk of progressing to end-stage renal disease (ESRD), nephrotic syndrome, or rapidly worsening disease [N2-R4]. Some guidelines also use the Kidney Failure Risk Equation (KFRE) to help decide when referral is appropriate, especially if the risk of needing kidney replacement therapy is >5% in the next 5 years [N1-F1].

Dialysis planning or specialized care becomes relevant when the disease moves closer to advanced stages or when the risk of needing dialysis rises. The evidence says dialysis is generally considered for stage 5 CKD, not stage 3 [N4-R1][N4-R3]. So, for stage 3, a specialist visit is more about slowing progression, managing complications, and planning for the future, not about starting dialysis [N2-F2][N1-F1].

At a specialist visit, you can expect a full review of your kidney function, urine protein, heart disease risk, and other complications. You may also get recommendations for lifestyle changes, diet, medications, and monitoring for anemia, mineral and bone disorder, metabolic acidosis, and high blood pressure [N2-F2]. In other words, the specialist helps you move from diagnosis to a personalized plan for slowing the disease.

## What local clinics and Lagos clinics can do

In Lagos, there are both general local clinics and specialized nephrology/dialysis centers available [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5][N6-R3][N6-R5]. The evidence shows that hospitals and centers such as Lagos State University Teaching Hospital (LASUTH), St. Raphael Divine Mercy Specialist Hospital, CardioCare Hospital, and other facilities offer nephrology consultations, dialysis services, and related treatments [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5][N6-R1]. These specialized centers can handle kidney biopsies, dialysis access, and other advanced services [N6-R1].

So, local clinics can help monitor routine kidney function and provide basic follow-up, but they may not be the best place to start specialist care for stage 3 disease. The evidence suggests that local clinics may not manage complications such as anemia, mineral and bone disorder, metabolic acidosis, or high blood pressure as comprehensively as a specialized nephrology center [N2-F2][N1-F1]. That means local clinics can be a good starting point, but specialist care is more appropriate when the diagnosis is confirmed and you need a full plan [N1-F1][N2-R4].

## What you can do now: next steps and questions

If you want to reduce uncertainty, ask your doctor these kinds of questions:  
- What stage does my eGFR put me in?  
- What caused my kidney disease?  
- Can I prevent further kidney damage?  
- What changes should I make to my lifestyle, diet, or medications?  
- What lab test results do I have, and have they changed since last time?  
- What will happen next, and how often should I be checked?  
- Should I see a nephrologist, and why? [N5-R3][N5-R5][N5-R4]

To track kidney function over time, focus on regular eGFR and urine albuminuria testing, because those are the main markers used to stage CKD and monitor progression [N1-R4][N1-F1]. The evidence also says that urine albuminuria is important even if not needed to confirm stage 3a CKD [N2-F2].

To prepare for a specialist visit, bring an updated list of medications, vitamins, supplements, and herbal medicines, and be ready to discuss lifestyle, diet, and any symptoms you are having [N5-R3][N5-R4]. Ask what tests the specialist will do and what they expect to find [N5-R1]. That way, you can go in with questions and a clearer picture of what comes next.

## Bottom line

Stage 3 kidney disease means your kidneys are moderately damaged, but dialysis is not yet needed [N1-R2]. Local clinics can manage early stage 3 as part of care, but specialist nephrology care is often needed when the diagnosis is established and risk is higher [N1-F1][N2-R4]. In Lagos, there are specialized nephrology and dialysis centers available, so your doctor can choose the best setting for your case [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5][N6-R1]. If you are unsure, the best next step is to ask your doctor what testing, monitoring, and specialist care are needed, and then prepare for a visit with specific questions [N5-R3][N5-R4].
